title: Jung
keyWorks: C. G. Jung, The Relations between the Ego and the Unconscious (1928)
C. G. Jung, The Stages of Life (1930)
C. G. Jung, The Archetypes of the Collective Unconscious (1934)
C. G. Jung, Psychology and Alchemy (1944)
C. G. Jung, Answer to Job (1952)
C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962)
C. G. Jung et al., Man and His Symbols (1964)
C. G. Jung, The Red Book (publ. 2009)
summary: Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961) was a Swiss psychiatrist and thinker who began alongside Freud and then created his own school, analytical psychology. For him the psyche is not a mechanism but a living whole that strives toward completeness. Jung studied dreams, myths, religions and alchemy and saw in them a shared language of images through which the depths of the human psyche speak. Here his ideas are presented as a philosophy of the soul — a way of understanding yourself, not a method of treatment.
onEmotions: Jung believed that the conscious “I” is only one part of the psyche, and that feelings often arrive from its unconscious layers as messages. Everything we don't accept in ourselves goes into the “Shadow”; the face we show the world he called the “persona”; and what we involuntarily see in others instead of in ourselves, “projection.” That's why Jung matters especially for “inconvenient” feelings — envy, schadenfreude, contempt, anger at loved ones: he shows that everyone has them and that they speak of unlived parts of the personality. The aim is neither to suppress them nor to act them out on others, but to become aware of them, moving toward “individuation” — becoming your whole self. Here we set out ideas, not clinical advice.

anxiety.text: Jung treated the soul's uninvited guests as messengers: first listen, then decide. Anxiety wears you out, and there's nothing shameful in it — but it, too, can be listened to. Jung saw the psyche as a self-regulating system: the unconscious — the part of our inner life that acts without our knowing — constantly “compensates” for the one-sidedness of consciousness. If we live for a long time from only one side of ourselves — say, controlling everything — then what has been left out comes back as a restlessness that seems to have no cause. It may be not a malfunction but a messenger: something in you is asking for attention. Jung suggested not chasing such states away but entering into dialogue with them — asking what image, what picture lives inside them. Sometimes anxiety turns out to have a face, and a face is something you can talk to.
anxiety.practice: Imagine your anxiety as a character and sit it in the chair opposite you: what does it look like, how old is it? Ask aloud: “What do you want to tell me?” — and hear the first answer without arguing.

fear.text: In December 1913 Jung sat at his desk and, in his words, decided to “let himself drop” — to fall into the depths of his own images. Fear is our oldest protection, and sometimes it's wise to listen to it; but Jung also knew another fear — of what we meet inside. In Memories, Dreams, Reflections he describes honestly how, after his break with Freud, from the end of 1913 he lived through years when images rose from the depths that frightened even him — and how he decided not to run but to write them down and paint them. Later these records became The Red Book. The lesson isn't heroism but attitude: what we turn away from grows in the dark, while what we can carefully look at takes on a shape and boundaries. A fear with a name and an outline is usually smaller than a faceless one.
fear.practice: Draw your fear the way Jung drew his images in The Red Book — scribbles or a single line will do. Give the drawing a name and notice whether anything has shifted in how it feels.

sadness.text: Jung compared psychic energy to a river: at times it goes underground, and the surface turns quiet and dry. Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and Jung wouldn't rush you out of it. He wrote that the soul lives by opposites: light and shadow, rising and descent, day and night. Jung called psychic energy “libido,” meaning not only desire but life force in general, and he noticed that at times it withdraws into the depths, “inward,” and less of it is left for consciousness. There, in the depths, quiet work is going on. Sadness, then, isn't empty time but a time when something is being digested and rebuilt. You can ask not “how do I make this stop?” but “what is changing in me right now?” The answer won't come at once, but the question lets you be with sadness rather than fight it.
sadness.practice: Before bed, put a slip of paper by your bed and write down one word for your feeling; in the morning, any image or fragment of a dream. Jung would say: set them side by side and don't interpret.

grief.text: Where does someone we loved go? Jung answered as a physician of the soul: among other places, inward. Jung lived through the death of his wife Emma in 1955. After her death he dreamed of her, and he added an upper story to his tower at Bollingen — as a sign that his life had to go on, but differently. Jung was convinced that the image of someone who has died lives on in the psyche: you can talk to them in your mind, remember them, ask their advice. Mourning is not only a loss but a rebuilding of the bond: the person is no longer beside you but begins to be present inwardly. This doesn't cancel the pain, but it makes it part of an ongoing relationship.
grief.practice: Set an empty chair beside you and say aloud one or two sentences to the person who has died — what you'd like to tell them now. Jung spoke like this with his inner figures: for him it was a way of continuing the bond.

loneliness.text: As a boy, Jung carved a little man from a ruler, hid him in the attic with a smooth stone, and told no one for years. That was how he coped with a loneliness that hurts — which isn't a sign that something is wrong with you. Jung knew it from childhood: as a boy he carried experiences he couldn't tell anyone about, and this made him lonely among people. Hence his observation: loneliness isn't the absence of people but the impossibility of sharing what matters to you. Jung saw another side: the path of “individuation” — becoming yourself, whole, not only convenient for others — passes through moments when no one fully understands you. This isn't a sentence to isolation but a sign that there is something of your own in you. When you find even one person able to hear it, the meeting can be especially deep.
loneliness.practice: Find a small smooth stone or any little object and hold it in your hand, as the boy Jung held his secret stone. Silently name one thing that matters to you but that you almost never talk about, and think about whom you might someday trust it to.

quote.text: Loneliness does not come from having no people about one, but from being unable to communicate the things that seem important to oneself, or from holding certain views which others find inadmissible.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

anger.text: As a schoolboy, fending off a gang, Jung grabbed one boy by the legs and swung him round, knocking the others over — and pondered the force that woke in him. Anger is a living force, and in itself it doesn't make you a bad person. Suppressing it simply sends it into the “Shadow” — Jung's name for the traits and impulses incompatible with our picture of ourselves. Banished there, anger doesn't disappear: it bursts out at the wrong moment or settles as bitterness. Acknowledged, it can become energy — the ability to say “no,” to protect a boundary, to stand up for what matters. Jung stressed that the Shadow holds not only darkness but much of the life force we lack. The question, then, isn't “how do I not get angry?” but “what is my anger protecting, and how can I give it a voice without harming anyone?”
anger.practice: Do something physical and safe — beat a rug, chop wood if you have any, walk fast — the way Jung chopped wood at Bollingen. With each effort, name to yourself what your anger is protecting: a boundary, a value, a hurt.

shame.text: Persona — that was the Roman word for an actor's mask, through which his voice sounded. Jung took the word for the face we show the world, and shame, when you want to hide completely, comes when that mask suddenly slips. Each of us wears such a persona: competent, decent, calm. The persona is necessary; it isn't a lie. But when something we don't accept in ourselves — the Shadow — shows through from beneath it, we feel shame, as if caught without our mask. Jung insisted that everyone has a Shadow: a person who cast no shadow would be not a saint but flat, lacking depth. Shame is a moment of meeting your own wholeness. It's painful, but it opens the possibility of being not perfect but real.
shame.practice: Tell yourself silently about what you'd like to hide: “This, too, is in me.” Put a palm on your chest and stay like that for a minute — Jung would call it inviting your own Shadow into the house.

guilt.text: Whose voice does your guilt speak in? Jung considered this one of the key questions. Guilt can be agonizing, and sometimes it points to something truly important. In a late essay on conscience (1958), Jung distinguished two of its voices. One is the internalized moral code: the rules of family, society, what is “done.” The other is a deeper, personal conscience that can diverge from the rules of those around you; Jung linked it with the Self — the deep wholeness of a person, which is wider than our conscious “I.” There is guilt for breaking other people's rules, and there is guilt for betraying yourself. So it helps not just to endure guilt but to work out whose language it speaks. Sometimes it's a reason to put something right. Sometimes it's a reason to stop punishing yourself for living your own life.
guilt.practice: Ask your guilt aloud: “Whose voice are you speaking in?” — and listen for the name, phrase or face it suggests. Then ask more quietly: “And what would my own conscience say?”

envy.text: Jung's followers coined the phrase “golden Shadow” for the bright things in us that we see only in others. Envy is unpleasant to admit, though almost everyone feels it, and here the Jungian view is unexpectedly comforting. Jung spoke of “projection”: we involuntarily see in others what actually belongs to us but hasn't yet been recognized. And what gets projected isn't only the dark but also the bright — unrealized abilities, courage, creative power — that very “golden Shadow.” When you envy someone, perhaps something shines in them that also lives in you but hasn't found a place in your life. Envy isn't proof of pettiness but a signpost: this is the direction your unlived life is reaching toward. The task isn't to take it from the other person but to recognize it in yourself.
envy.practice: Picture the person you envy and mentally borrow one quality from them — not a thing but a quality: courage, lightness, persistence. Try it on for a minute and ask: where in my life is there even a tiny sprout of this?

emptiness.text: The “afternoon” of life — that was Jung's name for its second half, when the morning's goals no longer warm you. Emptiness is a heavy, gray feeling, and it deserves gentle treatment. Jung wrote a lot about people whose lives are outwardly well arranged but who feel a lack of meaning. He noticed that this happens especially often in such an “afternoon”: the goals of youth — position, success, a settled household — have been reached or have lost their savor, and new ones haven't appeared yet. Emptiness isn't the absence of meaning altogether but the end of one meaning and a pause before another. Jung believed that in such periods a person is seeking a connection with the Self — with something larger than the familiar “I” and its tasks. You can give emptiness time: sometimes it's simply a cleared patch of ground where nothing has grown yet.
emptiness.practice: Sit for ten minutes doing nothing, the way Jung sat by the lake at Bollingen: look at water, clouds, or at least out of a window. Don't look for anything — let the cleared ground stay empty for a while.

quote.text: We cannot live the afternoon of life according to the programme of life's morning; for what was great in the morning will be little at evening, and what in the morning was true will at evening have become a lie.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

confusion.text: An almost forty-year-old physician builds a toy village out of stones on the shore of Lake Zurich — that is how Jung found his way through the most confused time of his life. When the old maps no longer work, confusion is genuinely disorienting. Jung went through this himself: after his break with Freud he, in his own words, lost his inner footing and didn't know where to go. Then he decided to trust what came from within — dreams, fantasies, play. Play, as in childhood, helped him feel out a direction. Jung saw such periods as the beginning of “individuation”: the old orientation is exhausted, the new one not yet born. Clarity doesn't always come from the effort of thinking: sometimes it's suggested by what you do with your hands, and with interest.
confusion.practice: Build something out of whatever is at hand — a little tower of pebbles, buttons, sugar cubes — for five minutes, with no goal, the way Jung did on the shore. Notice what thought comes along the way.

quote.text: Your vision will become clear only when you can look into your own heart. Who looks outside, dreams; who looks inside, awakes.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

fatigue.text: At Bollingen Jung had no electricity or telephone; he went there when he was tired of being “Professor Jung.” Tiredness is a signal, not a weakness. Jung saw the psyche as a system of energy: it has ebbs and flows, and what we spend doesn't come from nowhere. When we hold up a “persona” for a long time — the face we have to show at work or in the family — it takes a lot of strength, especially if the persona is far from what's inside. Jung warned against growing too tightly into your role: a person begins to live only as a function and quietly runs out of breath. Tiredness may be saying not only “you've done a lot” but also “you've been not quite yourself for too long.” Rest, then, isn't only sleep but also time when the mask can come off.
fatigue.practice: Take off one “mask” for half an hour: change into home clothes, switch off your work phone, and do something that belongs to no role — water a plant, make soup, sit on the balcony.

boredom.text: Jung noticed that a person's freshest energies hide where they are least skilled. Boredom seems trivial, but it can be very oppressive. Jung would see in it a stagnation of energy: when consciousness moves along a familiar rut, the life force he called “libido” stops flowing there and looks for another channel. In Psychological Types he described four basic ways of relating to the world — thinking, feeling, sensation and intuition. In each of us, some are developed and familiar while others remain in the shadow, clumsy and “childish.” But it's precisely there, according to Jung, that freshness and new possibilities are stored. Boredom is an invitation to where you are unskilled, where you are a beginner. That's often where a lost interest in life is hiding.
boredom.practice: Choose one activity for today that you're clearly clumsy at — drawing, singing, fixing, dancing — and do it for five minutes: badly, but with curiosity. Jung would call it a visit to the “inferior function.”

joy.text: “At Bollingen I am most deeply myself,” Jung wrote of his stone tower by the lake. Joy is beautiful, and it doesn't need to be tested for durability. Despite his interest in the dark sides of the soul, Jung prized the moments when a person feels alive and whole. He loved simple things: in his tower at Bollingen, which he built with his own hands, he chopped wood, cooked, pumped water — with no electricity or running water. For Jung, real joy often appears when the “I” and the deep Self are for a moment in agreement: when what you're doing matches who you are. Such joy is worth noticing and savoring, because it hints at where your path runs.
joy.practice: Do one simple thing today “the Bollingen way” — slowly and with your own hands: cook porridge, brew tea, boil water on the stove. Notice the moment when you and the task coincide.

love.text: Anima is Latin for “soul”; Jung gave this name to an inner image we often meet in another person before we come to know the person themselves. Love is one of the strongest forces of life, and Jung treated it with enormous respect. He noticed that falling in love often begins with “projection”: we see in the other an image that lives in our own soul. In men he called it the “anima,” in women the “animus”: an inner image of the “other,” our opposite, which makes a person irresistibly attractive. (Later Jungians understand these concepts more broadly, without tying them rigidly to sex.) Projection isn't deception: this is how a meeting begins. But mature love, for Jung, grows as we gradually tell apart where our inner image is and where the living person is — and go on loving that person. In this meeting, both are changed.
love.practice: Look at the person you love — or at their photo — as if for the first time, and find one trait that doesn't match your expectations. Stay with it for a minute: that is the living person behind the image.

quote.text: The meeting of two personalities is like the contact of two chemical substances: if there is any reaction, both are transformed.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

gratitude.text: Once a patient was telling Jung a dream about a golden scarab — and at that moment a beetle much like a scarab tapped at the office window. Jung called such coincidences “synchronicity,” and gratitude, which warms, often grows from a similar feeling: something came to us of its own accord. He said that our “I” is only a small part of the psyche, like an island in an ocean, and that most of our inner life happens without our knowledge and not by our will: dreams, insights, unexpected encounters. Inner and outer events sometimes line up so that a sense of meaning arises. Gratitude is the recognition that we don't do everything ourselves: something comes to us as a gift. Such recognition doesn't diminish you — it frees you: you stop carrying the weight of your life alone. And you begin to see how much has already been received.
gratitude.practice: Recall one encounter or chance event that changed your life even though you didn't plan it — your own “scarab at the window.” Say a short “thank you” to it aloud.

hope.text: “The transcendent function” sounds dry, but it names a lively hope: from two irreconcilable sides a third can be born. Hope is a quiet but stubborn force, and Jung gives it a serious foundation. He noticed that the psyche, like the body, strives toward balance and wholeness. When consciousness reaches a dead end, the unconscious often brings new images — in dreams, in fantasies, in unexpected thoughts. Jung explained: if you hold a contradiction within yourself for a long time without rushing to pick a side, a third thing can be born from that tension — a solution you couldn't have devised in advance. Hope isn't a naive expectation of a miracle but trust that work is still going on inside you, even when nothing changes outside. Sometimes a way out appears from where you least expected it.
hope.practice: Write down the contradiction you're stuck in as “both… and…” rather than “either… or…”, and put the note under your pillow. In the morning, look at it again: has a third thing appeared?

nostalgia.text: Jung wrote that in each of us lives an “eternal child” — an image that faces not backward but toward the future. Nostalgia is sweet and bitter at once, and there's nothing childish about it. Jung might say that what we long for isn't only a particular time. He wrote about “archetypes” — images and plots common to all people, held in the “collective unconscious,” the deepest layer of the psyche. One such image is paradise lost: childhood, home, a time when everything was whole. Nostalgia can be a touch of this archetype: the past glows brighter than it really was, because a longing for wholeness falls upon it. Jung himself, as a mature man, returned to childhood games and found in them a way forward. The past isn't only a loss but also a source from which to draw a lost quality: lightness, wonder, play.
nostalgia.practice: Play something from childhood for five minutes — pebbles, a paper airplane, a doodling game with a pencil. Jung would say: this is how a lost quality — lightness, wonder — comes back into today.

craving.text: In 1961, a few months before his death, Jung answered a letter from Bill Wilson, one of the founders of Alcoholics Anonymous. A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong, and Jung suggested looking at what lies behind it. In that letter he suggested that the craving for alcohol may be a low-level, distorted expression of a deep spiritual thirst — a person's striving for wholeness, for something larger than the everyday “I.” A craving isn't foolishness or vice: there is a genuine need in it that has simply found the wrong address. Jung didn't romanticize addiction — he saw how much suffering it brings — but he respected the thirst itself. A craving comes in a wave: it rises and subsides. While it's passing, you can ask: what do I really want?
craving.practice: When a wave of craving rises, sit down, put your feet on the floor and breathe, watching the wave the way Jung watched his images: where it is in your body, how it grows and subsides. Ask quietly: “What do I really want?”

addiction.text: “Spiritus contra spiritum” — three Latin words from Jung's letter which, Bill Wilson said, stood at the origins of Alcoholics Anonymous. Addiction is not a moral failure, and Jung was one of those who understood this. He spoke of “complexes” — knots in the psyche charged with strong feeling, which can act almost independently, as if taking possession of a person. Addiction can be seen this way: it's not that you are “weak,” but that a force larger than your conscious “I” has taken over. That's why willpower alone is often not enough. Hence his formula: against “spirits,” what helps is “spirit” — the experience of connection with something larger than yourself, and with other people. The way out isn't to shame yourself but not to remain alone with this force.
addiction.practice: Say aloud the name of a person or a mutual-help group where you'd be heard without judgment. Jung would say that “spirit” begins with connection to others; you don't have to call right now.

hangover.text: Jung said the Shadow is everything a person has no wish to be, and a hangover morning usually reminds us of it louder than an alarm clock. It's hard on body and soul: anxiety, shame, fragments of last night, and the inner accuser grows louder. The evening often lets the “persona” — your usual social mask — loosen, and what usually stays in the “Shadow” comes out: sharpness, frankness, clumsiness. In the morning the mask comes back and looks at what was done in horror. So the heaviness of the morning isn't only a bodily state but a meeting of two parts of you that don't know each other well. You don't need to sign the verdict a tired mind hands down. Big conclusions about yourself can wait until your strength returns; for now, simply take care of yourself as you would of someone who feels unwell.
hangover.practice: Tell yourself aloud: “No conclusions about myself today.” Then wash your face with cool water and open a window, as if letting the morning in to both of your parts — the mask and the Shadow.

euphoria.text: Jung took the word “inflation” from economics: literally, “puffing up.” With it he described highs when everything seems possible, helping us understand such moments without fear and without being blinded. Euphoria can simply be lived with gratitude. He described how the “I” sometimes overflows with a force that has come from the depths of the psyche and for a time identifies with it: it seems you can do anything and see right through everything. This energy itself is beautiful and real. Jung advised only remembering that it is larger than your “I” and doesn't wholly belong to it. This lets you enjoy the high and at the same time let important decisions rest a little. Euphoria is a gift best received with open palms rather than clenched in a fist.
euphoria.practice: Feel the high through your body — walk a little, open your palms as if holding something light without gripping it. Tell yourself: “This is bigger than me, and it will pass.” Put important decisions off to a calm day.

crash.text: “Enantiodromia,” running into the opposite: Jung loved this word of Heraclitus's because it describes life honestly. A sharp comedown after a high is a hard state, and it's not your fault. Its meaning is simple: every extreme sooner or later turns into its opposite. The higher the flight, the more noticeable the movement back. This isn't a punishment or proof that the joy was false — it's the rhythm of the psyche, its way of returning to balance. Jung believed that opposites don't cancel each other but together make up a whole: the day needs the night. The slump is part of the same wave as the high, and it too will pass. Right now it's more important not to pick yourself apart but to wait it out, as gently as you can, the way you wait out bad weather.
crash.practice: Put a hand on your belly and watch your breathing for a minute: the in-breath rises, the out-breath falls, and one turns into the other, as in Heraclitus. The slump is an out-breath; an in-breath will follow.

panic.text: In his hardest years Jung reminded himself of simple things: I have a family, a medical diploma, a house and an address — I am a real person in a real world. A panic attack is truly frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems something irreparable is about to happen. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Jung described how the “I” is sometimes flooded by forces of the psyche it can't take in all at once — as if a wave of the ocean washed over a small island. In the years of his own “confrontation with the unconscious,” he went through states in which he feared losing his footing, and he looked for it in the simplest things: family, work, everyday tasks. So what panic needs first of all is footing — bodily, concrete, here and now. Understanding will come later.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and say aloud, as Jung did: your name, your address, today's date. Then take a few breaths with the out-breath longer than the in-breath, feeling the support under your feet.

dread.text: Months before the First World War, Jung saw visions of a sea of blood over Europe and couldn't tell where the horror came from. Objectless dread, a heavy foreboding, is one of the most exhausting states, and you don't have to understand it right away. Jung thought a lot about what rises from the depths when a familiar world collapses. He wrote that what isn't made conscious inside is often experienced as fate advancing from outside — like a dark, formless cloud. Not necessarily because there's no threat, but because the fear doesn't yet have an image. Jung suggested giving an image to what is formless: drawing it, describing it, imagining it. What took on a form, he observed, stopped being all-consuming and became something one could relate to. Your state is neither a verdict nor a prophecy; it's something still searching for words.
dread.practice: Imagine this feeling as weather or a landscape and describe it aloud in three sentences: what sky, what light, what wind. Notice that you are looking at the landscape, not only standing inside it.

fomo.text: Jung used the phrase “unlived life” for what could have been ours but was left aside, and believed it doesn't vanish but seeks a way out. The fear of missing out is a recognizable feeling: it seems real life is happening somewhere else, and you're not there. Jung would say that “projection” is at work here: in other people's lives — pictures, stories, successes — we see our own unlived life. Besides, feeds are a world of “personas,” carefully built faces; comparing your living inner state with them is unfair from the start. Jung believed each person has their own path of “individuation,” and it can't be walked by copying someone else's. No one can live every life at once. The question, then, isn't “what am I missing?” but “what that I've seen truly resonates in me?” — that's a hint about your own path.
fomo.practice: Put your phone away and go out for ten minutes somewhere without a single “persona” from the pictures: a yard, a park, a river. On the way, ask yourself: what that I saw in the feed truly resonated in me?

sleepless.text: By day consciousness is a sentry at the gate; by night the sentry tires — Jung might describe sleeplessness this way. The night drags on, the thoughts seem darker than by day, and it's not your fault. At night consciousness grows tired of holding its defenses, and what was pushed aside during the day rises to the surface. He respected the night side of the psyche: dreams, half-asleep images, sudden thoughts are the language of the unconscious, which he saw not as an enemy but as a conversation partner. But a partner who speaks in images, not verdicts. So night thoughts shouldn't be taken as the final truth about your life: they're raw material, not a judgment. In the morning much looks different. If an image keeps returning, note it down and come back to it by day, when you're stronger.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, imagine telling the night thought at the gate: “Wait until morning; I'll come back to you in the daytime.” Then shift your attention to your breathing and the weight of the blanket.

betrayal.text: In 1913 Jung and Freud, until recently almost father and son, exchanged their last letters — and Jung spent years putting himself back together. Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but your picture of the world. The break with Freud was one of the most painful events of Jung's life. The Jungian James Hillman devoted an essay, “Betrayal,” to this theme. He suggested that betrayal is a bitter but common part of growing up: it destroys the “primal trust” in which we lived as children, protected from everything. Hillman also described dangerous responses to it — cynicism, revenge, refusing to trust at all. The pain of betrayal isn't meaningless: over time it can open up a more mature trust — not blind, but aware of vulnerability, and still not closed.
betrayal.practice: Write down what you believed before this event — about people, about yourself — and underline what you'd like to keep in a new, more mature form. Hillman would call it a trust that knows about vulnerability.

jealousy.text: When you love, Jung said, part of your own soul seems to move into another person. That's why jealousy burns and can't simply be switched off — but it can be looked at without shame. This is the “projection” of an inner image — the anima or animus. Then the threat of losing the person feels like the threat of losing a part of yourself — which is why it's so unbearable. This doesn't mean your feelings aren't real. It means that jealousy mixes fear for the relationship with fear for your own wholeness. It helps to ask: what exactly do I feel I would lose along with them? Sometimes the answer — a sense of your own worth, aliveness, meaning — points to something you can begin to grow in yourself, rather than handing it over entirely to someone else.
jealousy.practice: Imagine taking a part of your soul back from the jealous picture: name aloud one quality — aliveness, worth, tenderness — that you “gave” to this person, and say: “This is mine too.”

resentment.text: “It's not that we have complexes; complexes have us,” Jung quipped. Resentment that won't go away is a heavy load, and there are usually serious reasons for it. Jung would call it a “complex” — a knot of experiences charged with strong feeling. Complexes live an almost independent life: touch them, and they replay the old scene again and again, as if it were happening now. Resentment isn't pettiness but a wound that hasn't yet found a way out and keeps repeating its story. Relief comes not from forcing yourself to “forgive” but from acknowledging the pain fully — and then it can gradually loosen its grip.
resentment.practice: Tell it aloud — to an empty room or someone close — as one connected story: what was done to you and what it meant to you. Not for forgiveness or revenge: a complex weakens once it has been heard to the end.

heartbreak.text: Falling in love, for Jung, is like a light kindled in our own soul suddenly shining in another person. A broken heart hurts almost physically, and there's no need to hurry to “let go.” Jung might say that along with the person, what we “projected” onto them leaves too: the inner image of the beloved, which he called the anima or animus. While the love lasted, this image lived outside, in another person. Now it's as if it returns to you — and at first it feels like emptiness and a wound. But for Jung this is also an opportunity: to notice that what you loved so much in the other — tenderness, courage, depth — was partly sounding in you as well. This doesn't devalue either the love or the person. It means that they have gone, but not all the good that woke up in you beside them.
heartbreak.practice: Name aloud three qualities you loved most in this person, placing a hand on your heart with each: which of them lives, at least a little, in you too?

impostor.text: “No. 1” and “No. 2” — that is what the teenage Jung called the two personalities he sensed in himself. When it feels as if you're about to be exposed, it's agonizing — and Jung understood well where the feeling comes from. Jung would describe this through the concept of the “persona” — the social mask, the face we go out into the world with: job title, status, role. The persona is necessary, but it never coincides with the whole person, and in the gap between them arises the feeling “I'm not who they think I am.” His “No. 1” was a schoolboy trying to measure up; “No. 2,” someone older and deeper. Feeling like an impostor isn't proof of deceit but a sign that you are more than your role. No one fully coincides with their persona, not even those who seem confident.
impostor.practice: Tell someone close about one of your work doubts — not for comfort, but to let “No. 2” speak aloud. Often it turns out others know the same gap between themselves and their role.

self_hatred.text: “What if I should discover that I myself am the enemy who must be loved?” Jung asked. When an inner voice insists that you're worthless, it hurts terribly — and that voice is wrong, however convincing it sounds. Jung would most likely see in it not the truth about you but a “complex” — an old knot of experience that speaks in other people's words and plays the same record over and over. He also believed that everything we can't accept in ourselves goes into the “Shadow,” and the more fiercely we fight it, the louder it makes itself heard. Jung suggested not fighting yourself but gradually acknowledging: yes, this is in me too, and I am still a person worthy of life and care. Acceptance here isn't approval of everything; it's giving up the war with yourself.
self_hatred.practice: Rest a hand on your own shoulder, as you would on a friend's, and say aloud one sentence you would say to them in your place. Jung would call it the alms of your own kindness.

quote.text: We cannot change anything unless we accept it. Condemnation does not liberate, it oppresses.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

helplessness.text: Jung compared the conscious “I” to a small island in the ocean of the psyche. Helplessness is one of the hardest feelings: it seems nothing depends on you, and Jung wouldn't try to persuade you that you're all-powerful. On the contrary, he stressed that the conscious “I” is only part of the psyche, and it really doesn't control everything: not dreams, not moods, not many events. But from this he drew a conclusion not of powerlessness but of alliance. If the “I” can't cope on its own, it can lean on a wider wholeness that Jung called the Self — on that in you which goes on living, seeking and recovering, even when you don't feel it. Helplessness isn't the end of the road but the place where your usual means run out and small steps and patience begin.
helplessness.practice: Do one very small thing that is in your hands — as Jung returned to simple tasks on hard days: make tea, open a window, straighten a blanket. The island is still there.

procrastination.text: Jung said the psyche has a will of its own — and sometimes it shows itself simply: the task doesn't get done. Putting things off isn't always laziness, and it's worth looking at more closely. The psyche's will doesn't always coincide with the will of the “I.” If some part of you resists a task, that resistance may be telling you something: the task isn't yours, it was imposed; it frightens you; or something else is needed right now. Jung would call such parts “complexes” — they have their own feelings and their own logic, and they know how to sabotage the plans of consciousness. Fighting procrastination by willpower alone is like arguing with someone without listening to them. Better to ask: who in me doesn't want to do this, and why? Sometimes, once heard, this inner voice agrees to at least the first step.
procrastination.practice: Imagine the part of you that's putting the task off and ask it aloud: “What are you afraid of, or what do you want instead?” Hear the answer and offer a deal: just the first step, five minutes.

uprooted.text: For more than thirty years Jung built, with his own hands, a stone tower on the shore of Lake Zurich — a home that, he said, connected him with his ancestors. Being cut off from home, from your land and your language, is a real loss. Jung gave roots enormous importance. He was convinced that beneath personal memory lies a deeper layer — the “collective unconscious,” a psychic soil shared by all people, filled with ancient images. Being torn from a familiar place lays this depth bare: outer supports disappear, and you have to look for roots within. At Bollingen he felt connected with many centuries at once. Home isn't only an address but something you can recreate piece by piece: objects, rituals, words that hold you wherever you are.
uprooted.practice: Place one stone, object or photo from your old home on a windowsill or table — like the first stone of your own “tower.” Next to it, do something familiar from there: brew tea the way you did at home.

overload.text: Jung lived long before smartphones, but already in the 1930s he warned that modern people live too much “on the outside.” Overload from an endless stream is a real burden, not a flaw of yours. Modern people, for Jung, are identified with consciousness, external events and demands, and cut off from inner life. He considered this one of the ills of our culture. To restore balance, Jung himself would go off to Bollingen, where he had neither electricity nor a telephone, and where, in his words, he was most himself. Overload is a signal that there's too much of the outer and nowhere for the inner to be heard. You don't need your own Bollingen — a few minutes of silence that the stream can't reach will do.
overload.practice: Turn off all screens and sounds for five minutes — make yourself a small Bollingen. Just sit and notice what image or thought appears first when it gets quiet.

unreality.text: In his strangest times Jung did the most ordinary things: worked stone, cooked, talked with those close to him. The feeling of unreality — as if the world or you yourself were behind glass — is a strange and disturbing experience. Jung took such states seriously and without condescension. In the years of his “confrontation with the unconscious,” he himself went through periods when the boundary between inner images and the outer world grew shaky. So as not to get lost, he held tightly to the most ordinary things: family, work, his daily routine. In the Memories he writes that these simple realities were an anchor for him, reminding him that he existed in the real world. For Jung, the “I” is only part of a wider psyche, and sometimes it temporarily weakens. It can be helped by the simplest things: a touch, handiwork, the voice of someone close.
unreality.practice: For a minute or two, do the most everyday task with your hands — wash a cup, fold a towel — naming each movement aloud: “picking up,” “warm water,” “drying.” The everyday is the best anchor.

awe.text: “Vocatus atque non vocatus deus aderit” — “Called or not called, the god will be present”: Jung had these words carved over the door of his house. Awe is a rare and precious feeling, and it doesn't need to be fully explained. Jung took from the theologian Rudolf Otto the word “numinous” — the experience of something vast, at once frightening and fascinating, before which a person feels small and intensely alive. Jung considered such experiences among the most important in the soul's life: in them the “I” touches something larger than itself. He wrote that numinous experience can change a life, because it gives a sense of meaning that can't be reached by reasoning. Awe before the sea, a starry sky, music or the birth of a child is a moment when you meet the depth of the world and your own depth at the same time.
awe.practice: Read aloud the words over Jung's door: “Called or not called, the god will be present.” Then stay a minute with whatever filled you with awe, doing nothing, and name in one word what you have met.

relief.text: “The psyche is a self-regulating system,” Jung kept saying, and relief is perhaps the best proof of it. It comes when what held you for a long time lets go, and it's worth simply living it. Jung would note that relief often comes when the tension between opposites is finally resolved: for a long time you were pulled in different directions — and suddenly a way out appeared, or time simply did its work. He wrote that the psyche, like the body, strives for balance, and this striving doesn't need our effort every minute — sometimes it does its work on its own. It is a sign that your inner self-regulation is working. It's a good moment to notice: you got through it, and there's a strength in you that helped you do so. It's worth remembering for the future.
relief.practice: Stretch your whole body, as after sitting for a long time, and on the out-breath say: “That's behind me.” Notice where in your body the relief is strongest — that is where balance is at work right now.

calm.text: In 1918–1919 Jung drew a small circle — a mandala — in a notebook every morning and read in it how he was that day. Calm is a precious state, and it's worth valuing without waiting for a catch. Jung saw deep calm as a moment when the “I” and the Self — the deep center of the personality — are in agreement. His symbol of such wholeness was the mandala, a circular pattern found in the most diverse cultures. He realized that the mandala expresses the psyche's striving toward a center and balance. Your calm isn't an accidental pause but an expression of the wholeness the soul strives for. You can remember it so you can return to it.
calm.practice: Draw a circle and, inside it, whatever comes right now, as Jung did every morning. Let it be the mandala of your calm.

inspiration.text: Philemon was the name of an old man with a kingfisher's wings who appeared to Jung in fantasies and said things Jung himself didn't know. Inspiration is a joyful state in which ideas seem to come by themselves, and Jung believed that, in part, they do. In his writings on artistic creation he distinguished two paths: sometimes the author guides the work consciously, and sometimes the work seems to grow on its own, using the person as an instrument, and then it says more than the author's personal experience. Inspiration is a meeting with the creative power of the unconscious, and you needn't claim it as your own — you can receive it with gratitude. This takes the pressure off: you don't have to invent everything yourself; it's enough to listen carefully and write it down.
inspiration.practice: Imagine your own “Philemon” — an inner conversation partner who knows more than you — and ask him aloud a question about your idea. For five minutes, capture his answers as they come, without editing.

schadenfreude.text: “One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making the darkness conscious,” Jung wrote. Schadenfreude is unpleasant to discover in yourself, though almost everyone has felt it at least once. Jung would say it's the voice of the “Shadow” — the part of us that stores everything that doesn't fit the image of a “good person”: rivalry, resentment, the wish to come out on top. Everyone has a Shadow, and Jung believed it's far more dangerous not to know your Shadow than to know it. Schadenfreude often speaks of hidden pain: a feeling of having been underestimated or passed over, a secret comparison in which you long came off worse. The feeling itself says nothing final about you. What matters is not pretending it isn't there, but asking what wound it covers — and not letting it steer your actions.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself aloud, without judgment: “Where did this person once hurt me, or in what do I compare myself with them?” The first answer is a piece of Shadow brought into the light.

quote.text: One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, but by making the darkness conscious.
quote.author: Carl Gustav Jung

contempt.text: In Aion, Jung wrote that projections turn our surroundings into a reflection of our own unknown face. Contempt is a cold feeling, and it's not easy to admit to. Jung would point out how often it's linked to “projection” — involuntarily attributing to another person what we don't accept in ourselves. The more hotly some trait in a person gets to us — weakness, stupidity, smugness — the more likely it is that it somehow concerns us too: perhaps we are suppressing it in ourselves with all our might. This doesn't mean the other person is blameless. It means that contempt carries information about you as well. It isn't a reason to feel superior but a chance to learn something important about yourself.
contempt.practice: Name aloud the trait you despise in this person, then quietly ask: “When am I afraid of discovering this in myself?” Look at the answer as your own “unknown face.”

disgust.text: The alchemists Jung studied all his life had a saying: the gold is found in dung — in stercore invenitur. Disgust is a strong bodily feeling that often protects you and is perfectly reasonable, but the alchemists also knew the value of the “low.” Jung would also suggest looking at what exactly gets to us so much. The “Shadow,” in his view, gathers everything we consider low, dirty, animal in ourselves, and disgust at something outside sometimes guards the border against that inner something. It's especially hard when disgust is turned on yourself. Then it helps to remember: Jung believed that wholeness includes the “low,” the bodily, the imperfect — without it a person is not purer but poorer. Disgust should neither be obeyed like an order nor be a source of shame. You can ask: what border is it guarding right now — and do I need that border?
disgust.practice: Notice where in your body the disgust lives, place your palm there and breathe for a minute without trying to get rid of it. Like an alchemist over a flask, simply watch what happens to the “low” matter.

revenge.text: Jung compared an archetype to a riverbed: water flowed in it for centuries, and when rain comes, the stream finds the old course. Revenge runs in an ancient bed: when you've been hurt, a demand for justice rises — yet the wish isn't an act and doesn't make you a bad person. In such moments we can be seized by an “archetype,” here the ancient plot of retribution, which pulls you along like a current. When an archetype “possesses” a person, they begin to act not as themselves but as a character in an old tragedy. Jung believed that the way out lies in awareness: once you see the plot, you don't have to play your part in it. The thirst for revenge speaks of a real wound and a violated boundary. They need a path that protects you and restores your dignity without harming anyone.
revenge.practice: Fill a glass with water and slowly pour it into the sink, imagining the old riverbed of revenge running dry. Then say aloud what you really need: acknowledgment of your pain, protection, an apology.

anger_at_loved.text: Jung wrote that where love is strong, its opposite is never far: the psyche works in pairs. Anger at a partner, parents, children is one of the feelings we're most ashamed of, but it doesn't cancel love. The stronger the attachment, the more hidden tension it holds. Those close to us touch our “complexes” — old, charged knots — because it was with people like them that we once learned to love and to be hurt. We also often see our parents' traits in a partner, and transfer our own unlived life onto our children. Anger at a loved one is a sign of a strong bond and a reason to understand which old knot has been touched. You don't have to pour it out on the person; you can find words for it once the wave has settled.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger has subsided, say aloud to yourself: “It hurt me so much because it's like…” — and finish it. Jung would call this looking for the old knot the person touched.

ambivalence.text: The emblem of Jungian psychology is a union of opposites: sun and moon, king and queen in the alchemical flask. Loving and not being able to stand someone, wanting to be close and wanting to leave: such mixed feelings are very hard, but entirely human. Jung, perhaps more than most, valued the capacity to hold opposites. He believed the psyche is polar in structure: light and shadow, love and aggression, closeness and separateness. Trying to keep only one side makes a person one-sided, and the repressed side comes back anyway. Jung described the “transcendent function”: if you patiently hold both feelings within you, without forcing yourself to choose one, a third thing can in time be born — a new, more mature attitude. Your ambivalence isn't a sign of a bad relationship but the honesty of a soul that sees the person whole.
ambivalence.practice: Hold something warm in one hand and something cool in the other, say a cup of tea and a glass of water, for a minute. Both hands are yours, as are both feelings; neither has to be let go right now.

guilty_relief.text: You can't forbid the out-breath after holding your breath for a long time, and Jung believed the soul has such an out-breath too. Relief after a breakup, after leaving a grueling job, even after the death of a loved one who was long ill often comes with shame, but relief and love can live together. Jung repeated insistently that the psyche doesn't obey the rules of “proper” feelings: opposites sound in it at the same time. Long tension, caregiving and fear drain your strength, and when it ends, the soul breathes out — this isn't betrayal but its natural self-regulation. The shame here speaks in the voice of the “persona” — ideas about what one is supposed to feel. Relief doesn't cancel your love, grief and faithfulness. It only shows how hard it was for you — and that you got through it.
guilty_relief.practice: Hold your breath for a few seconds and slowly breathe out — there it is, the out-breath no one can forbid. On the out-breath, say: “I feel lighter, and my love hasn't become any smaller because of it.”

indifference.text: “The way it should be” — in those words, for Jung, it's the persona speaking, not the living person. Indifference where something “should” move you is frightening: it seems something is wrong with you. Jung would suggest not rushing to a verdict. In his view, psychic energy — “libido” in the broad sense, simply life force — isn't always where consciousness expects it. Sometimes it withdraws into the depths, where quiet work is going on; sometimes it's taken up by tiredness or long strain; sometimes it reaches toward something quite other than what's “expected.” Indifference isn't proof of callousness but information: there's no energy here right now, and it may be somewhere else. Feelings often return once you stop trying to squeeze them out of yourself.
indifference.practice: Go outside or to a window and for a minute look for anything that touches you even slightly: a color, a sound, someone's face — even if it's not at all what it “should” be. Name it aloud, without judgment: this shows where the energy has gone.

escape.text: Marie-Louise von Franz described people who live a “provisional life”: the real present is about to begin — somewhere else, after a move. The urge to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — isn't shameful, and Jungians take it seriously. They speak of the “eternal youth,” the puer aeternus, whom von Franz described in detail. It's the part of us that thirsts for freedom, novelty, life without limits. Von Franz also saw the trap in it. But the Jungian view sees something else in the urge to escape: perhaps the “persona,” the role you play, has become too tight, and the soul is demanding room. The important question is: what exactly am I running from, and toward what? The dream of escape deserves a hearing: there's truth in it about what you lack.
escape.practice: Imagine you're already where you want to run to, and name aloud three sensations: what you see, what you hear, what the air is like. These three words are about what you lack here; which of them could you let into this week?

forbidden_attraction.text: In fairy tales Jungians liked to interpret, the hero often falls in love with a portrait — the image of someone he has never seen. Attraction to someone who is “off limits” — unavailable, or the “wrong” person — is embarrassing and unsettling. Jung wouldn't pass moral verdicts here; he'd ask what this attraction says about the soul. For Jung, a strong, seemingly causeless attraction is often tied to the “projection” of the anima or animus — the inner image of the “other” living in our psyche. Such an image carries what conscious life lacks: passion, freedom, depth, recognition. And the less of these there is in everyday life, the more brightly the image flares up on someone outside. The attraction isn't only about the other person but also about an unrecognized part of yourself. It can be explored inwardly — in thoughts, dreams, writing — and that exploration is valuable in itself.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Picture a framed portrait of this person and step back from it: what one quality shines in the portrait — passion, freedom, depth? Ask: where in my life is there no room for this quality right now?

social_anxiety.text: “Introvert” and “extravert” — words everyone knows today — were brought into wide use by Jung. Fear of other people's judgment is a common and painful feeling, and Jung helps you look at it more calmly. An introvert is turned first of all toward the inner world, an extravert toward the outer, and neither type is better than the other. Shyness and introversion aren't the same thing, but they are often intertwined. Jung himself was more of an introvert, and in the Memories he admits that in childhood and youth he felt alien and awkward among his peers. He noticed that Western culture values the extraverted style more, and it's easy for an introvert to decide that something is wrong with them. Your sensitivity to people isn't a defect but a trait that needs its own pace and its own space.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, plan yourself a small “refuge” — a minute by the window or a quick step outside — and walk there in your mind in advance. An introvert needs a Bollingen of their own, even if only for a minute.

uncertainty.text: For years Jung and the physicist Wolfgang Pauli corresponded about an order in the world that can't be predicted. Uncertainty wears you out: it's unclear what will happen, and there's nothing to lean on. Jung would say that consciousness strives for clarity and control, while the life of the psyche and of the world is much wider than what we can foresee. He used the word “synchronicity” for cases when inner and outer events unexpectedly coincide in meaning, and the very concept was an admission: there is an order in the world that can't be reduced to our plans. Uncertainty isn't only a threat but also a space in which something may appear that you couldn't have planned. This doesn't cancel the anxiety. But you can stop demanding that you know the future and stay attentive to what comes along the way.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don't know what will happen with…” — and beside it: “But I know that today I can…”. Read both lines aloud: one small certainty against a background of great unknown.

waiting.text: Jonah spends three days in the belly of the whale — Jung saw in this story a “night sea journey,” a time when nothing happens outside. Waiting for an answer, results, news drags on agonizingly, and time seems to freeze. Jung wrote a lot about symbols of transition: in myths and fairy tales the hero often goes through a period of being locked up, swallowed, cut off from the world. Outwardly nothing happens in such days, but inside a change is being prepared. Waiting is a burdensome but not empty time. It's an in-between state in which you are no longer who you were, but don't yet know who you'll become. Jung didn't promise that the outcome would necessarily be good. But he helps you see that even while waiting, you are living, not only waiting.
waiting.practice: Walk for ten minutes, imagining that you're on a “night sea journey”: quiet outside, while something ripens within. In those minutes, allow yourself to live and not only to wait.

regret.text: Jung was convinced that what we miss doesn't vanish from the psyche: unlived possibilities wait in the Shadow like shoots that lacked light. Regret over what you did or didn't do can hold on for a long time. Jung might note that over the years we regret not only particular actions but also unlived sides of ourselves. In “The Stages of Life” he wrote that the second half of life offers a chance to turn toward what was cast aside in the first for the sake of success and adapting to the world. Regret isn't only pain about the past but also a signpost: what of what was lost still wants to live. Much can't be brought back in its old form, but the quality behind it can sometimes be let into today.
regret.practice: Put a seedling, a flower or just a glass of water on the windowsill and name aloud the quality that stood behind what didn't happen: courage, tenderness, play. Think where that shoot could get a little light this week.

longing.text: “Active imagination” — that was Jung's name for a waking, serious conversation with inner images. Longing for a particular person aches quietly and constantly, as if there were an empty place in your heart in their shape. For Jung, someone close lives not only outside but also inside us — as an image, a voice, a part of our psyche. When the person is far away, this inner image keeps sounding, and longing is its call. Jung valued this practice and advised writing such conversations down. So the bond isn't broken by distance: it can be kept up inwardly while an outward meeting isn't possible. This doesn't replace the living person, but it helps longing be not only a wound but also a form of faithfulness.
longing.practice: Write a few lines as if you were talking with this person in “active imagination”: what you would say to them, and what you imagine they would answer. Don't edit — let the image speak for itself.

world_pain.text: Jung wrote Answer to Job almost feverishly, while ill; the book, he said, “came” to him. Pain for the world — from heavy news, wars, injustice — speaks of your capacity for compassion. Jung lived through two world wars and thought a great deal about evil. In his late book Answer to Job (1952) he returned to the biblical story of a righteous man who suffers without guilt, and he didn't smooth it over: Job's suffering can't be explained by anything he deserved. For Jung this was a question of how a person can bear evil without closing their eyes to it. He also believed that the capacity for destruction exists in everyone, and knowing this is the first protection. Carrying pain for the world means seeing the darkness and guarding the light in yourself, not letting despair make you numb.
world_pain.practice: Put a hand on your heart and admit aloud: “I'm hurting for the world.” Then do one small kind thing within reach today — your own piece of light beside the darkness.

rejection.text: The persona is a mask, not a face: Jung insisted on this difference all his life. Rejection wounds deeply: it seems it wasn't an offer or a job that was turned down but you yourself — this difference helps here. He distinguished the “persona” — how we present ourselves to others — from the whole personality, which includes both the Shadow and the deep Self. A refusal usually concerns a meeting at the level of personas: your role and how well it matched the other's expectations. It can't pass judgment on you as a whole. Jung would also say that rejection is especially painful when it touches an old “complex” — an early experience where we already felt unwanted — and then the new pain is amplified by the old. You can feel compassion both for yourself today and for the one who once went through this for the first time.
rejection.practice: Say aloud, slowly, twice: “What was turned down was my… (offer, letter, confession), not all of me.” The persona got the “no,” not the whole of you.

abandonment.text: Moses was left in a basket on the river, Hansel and Gretel in the forest — and Jung noticed that the abandoned child of myth almost always survives. The fear of being abandoned is one of the most ancient human fears, and it deserves gentleness. Jung saw “archetypes” in the depths of the psyche — images and plots common to all people. One of them is the abandoned child. In the essay “The Psychology of the Child Archetype” (1940), Jung observed that abandonment in these stories is not only a misfortune but also a condition of future strength: the abandoned child survives and grows up. Your fear touches something very early. But there is also a part of you that knows how to survive and to care for your own vulnerability — for the “inner child.”
abandonment.practice: Wrap your arms around your shoulders and say the words you would have wanted to hear as a child, when you were afraid of being left alone. Jung would say you are speaking with your “inner child.”

unrequited.text: Part of the radiance we see in the one we love comes from ourselves — a bitter thought of Jung's, but a consoling one too. Unrequited love is bitter: everything inside you is turned toward a person, and there's no answer. When we fall deeply in love, we, in his view, “project” onto the other the anima or animus — the inner image of an ideal “other” living in our soul. Hence the strength of the feeling, and the sense that without this person life loses its color. Projection doesn't make the love unreal: your feelings are genuine. Unrequited love is also a meeting with your own capacity to love, which doesn't disappear even if it finds no answer right now. Little by little, this light can be brought back to yourself and your life.
unrequited.practice: Light a candle or switch on a small lamp and say aloud what this love awakens in you: tenderness, inspiration, courage. That light is yours, and it can go on burning regardless of any answer.

humiliation.text: Jung distinguished the mask from the face: a persona can be torn off, but the Self doesn't come off with it. Humiliation is one of the most searing experiences: as if stripped of your dignity in front of others. Jung would say that in such a moment the “persona” has been torn off — the face we show the world, which protects our vulnerability. Being left without it is frightening. But Jung stressed that a person isn't the same as their persona: dignity lives deeper, in what he called the Self, and it doesn't depend on others' words and looks. He observed that the collapse of the persona sometimes becomes the beginning of a new, more honest relationship with yourself. This in no way excuses those who humiliated you. Your pain speaks of a value that was hurt — and that value is still yours.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, straighten your shoulders and slowly lift your chin, as if putting on not a mask but your own face. Say aloud one sentence about what in you has remained unchanged.

body_shame.text: At Bollingen Jung cut stone, chopped wood and hauled water, and in these simple efforts his body was not a picture but an ally. Dissatisfaction with your body can be agonizing and very personal. For Jung, the body often ends up in the “Shadow” of our culture: for centuries spirit was placed above flesh, and now the body is often judged as a thing that must match a template. Jung, though, believed that human wholeness is impossible without the bodily, the “low,” the imperfect and alive. He saw the body not as a facade but as the home of the soul. We also often carry other people's judgments, heard long ago, that sound like our own voice. Your body isn't a project to be fixed but a part of you that has been carrying your life all this time.
body_shame.practice: Make one simple physical effort, as at Bollingen: carry something heavy, sweep the floor, stretch your arms. Then name three things your body did for you today.

illness.text: Jung called psyche and body two sides of one reality, so when your body lets you down, your whole life feels it: the familiar sense of strength collapses, and it becomes frightening. Jung knew this firsthand: in 1944, after breaking his leg, he had a heart attack and recovered slowly. In Memories, Dreams, Reflections he writes that after the illness he understood how important it is to accept one's fate and say “yes” to what is — and that it was then that a fruitful period began for him: he wrote many of his major books after it. Illness is neither a defeat nor a punishment but a hard event that touches your whole life, and a new relationship with yourself can be born in it too. This isn't about replacing treatment, but about how the soul can live through what is happening.
illness.practice: Ask yourself aloud not “why is this happening to me?” but “what do I need most right now?” — and do one small act of self-care: a blanket, a warm drink, a call to someone close.

pride.text: At Bollingen Jung carved inscriptions about his life and work into a stone — and left it on the shore among the trees, not in a museum. Pride in what you've done is a healthy and well-earned feeling, and it's worth living it fully. For Jung, it's a recognition that your “I” has done its job: endured, created, seen something through to the end. He warned only against one trap, which he called “inflation” — when the “I” starts identifying with something larger than it is, and confuses its success or its role with the whole of itself. Healthy pride knows its measure and remembers that the strength came not only from you but also from the psyche's depths, other people, circumstances. That's why it can be joy and gratitude at once. Such pride doesn't puff you up; it makes you stronger.
pride.practice: Take a pebble or any small object and in your mind “carve” one word on it about what you've done. Put it somewhere visible and name aloud one person or circumstance that helped.

melancholy.text: Nigredo, “blackening,” was the alchemists' name for the darkness with which every transformation begins. Gentle sadness is a subtle and deep state, and it doesn't need fixing. Jung would probably see in it the soul turning inward — an “introversion” of energy, when the outer world recedes for a while and the inner world grows brighter. Jung long studied alchemy as a language of symbols of inner transformation. The alchemists associated this stage with melancholy. It wasn't a defeat but a necessary step of the work. Jung considered this image an accurate description of what happens in the soul: descent into dusk precedes a new light. Melancholy is a time of ripening. You can stay in it, as in a quiet twilight, listening.
melancholy.practice: Sit for a few minutes in the twilight without turning on the light — with quiet music or simply by a window. Then name aloud one word: what is ripening in you now.
